questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with sudden swelling, erythema of existing skin patches, and new patches appearing over 3 days. Nerve tenderness is noted at the ulnar nerve. There is no fever or tender nodules. What is the most likely type of reaction occurring?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) reaction occurring in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL). It presents with sudden inflammation of existing patches, new patches, and nerve tenderness without systemic symptoms. ENL occurs in BL/LL leprosy and features tender erythematous nodules with systemic fever. Lucio phenomenon is a necrotizing arteritis in untreated diffuse lepromatous leprosy. Treatment: prednisolone 40mg/day tapered over 6 months.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae on the trunk and scalp, and painful oral erosions for 2 months. Nikolsky sign is positive. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis with a row of tombstone basal cells. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits in a chicken-wire pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, suprabasal acantholysis (tombstone appearance of basal cells), and intercellular IgG deposits (chicken-wire pattern) on DIF against desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 in severe disease). Oral mucosa is involved in >90%. Bullous pemphigoid shows tense bullae, subepidermal cleavage, and linear BMZ deposits. DH shows granular IgA at dermal papillae tips.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man presents with tense bullae on erythematous urticarial plaques affecting the trunk and proximal limbs. Oral mucosa is spared. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. Which structural antigen is the primary target?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies against BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230, both components of the hemidesmosome. This leads to subepidermal cleavage and tense bullae. Oral involvement is uncommon (<30%). DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Desmoglein 3 and 1 are targeted in pemphigus vulgaris. Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils below the lamina densa) is the target in dystrophic EB and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active male presents with a painless, non-pruritic copper-colored maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles. He recalls a painless penile ulcer 7 weeks ago that healed spontaneously. Generalized lymphadenopathy is present. VDRL titre is 1:64 and TPHA is reactive. What stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis appears 4-8 weeks after the primary chancre heals. Classic features include a copper-colored maculopapular rash on palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, condylomata lata (moist warty perigenital plaques), mucous patches, and split papules at oral commissures. VDRL is strongly positive. Treatment: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose.

questions.q: A 22-year-old college student presents with hypopigmented, finely scaly macules on the chest and back that fail to tan in summer. Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence. KOH mount reveals short curved hyphae and round thick-walled spores (spaghetti and meatballs appearance). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (also called Pityrosporum orbiculare). The pathognomonic KOH mount shows short hyphae and round spores - the 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. Hypopigmentation results from azelaic acid production inhibiting tyrosinase. Golden-yellow fluorescence on Wood's lamp is characteristic. Treatment: topical ketoconazole shampoo, selenium sulfide, or oral itraconazole/fluconazole for extensive cases.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped photosensitive rash on the malar region sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, and discoid lesions. ANA is 1:640 (homogeneous). Anti-dsDNA titre is elevated. Which autoantibody is considered the MOST SPECIFIC for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (Smith) antibodies are the most specific for SLE (specificity ~99%), targeting snRNP proteins. Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific (~95-99%) and correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis. Anti-histone antibodies are the hallmark of drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid). Anti-Ro/SSA is found in subacute cutaneous LE, neonatal lupus, and Sjogren syndrome. Anti-Sm is pathognomonic though less sensitive (25-30%).

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope discoloration of the eyelids with periorbital edema, Gottron's papules over the MCP joints, V-sign erythema, and periungual telangiectasias. Serum CK is 5200 U/L. What is the most important condition to rule out in this patient?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis has a well-established paraneoplastic association in 15-30% of adult cases. Risk increases with age (>50 years), anti-TIF1-gamma antibodies, and absence of anti-Jo-1. Associated malignancies include ovarian, lung, gastric, colorectal, and nasopharyngeal cancers (especially in Asian patients). All adult DM patients require comprehensive age-appropriate cancer screening with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, gynecologic evaluation, and tumor markers.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man has a changing pigmented lesion on his back. Excision biopsy confirms melanoma with Breslow thickness 2.5 mm, no ulceration, Clark level IV. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is negative. What is the recommended surgical excision margin for definitive wide local excision?
questions.exp: Surgical margins for melanoma by Breslow thickness: in situ = 0.5-1 cm; <1 mm = 1 cm; 1-2 mm = 1-2 cm; >2 mm = 2 cm. For this 2.5mm thick melanoma, a 2 cm margin is recommended. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered for Breslow >0.8mm (or ulcerated melanoma >=0.8mm). Adjuvant immunotherapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) or targeted therapy (BRAF/MEK inhibitors for BRAF V600E) is considered for high-risk stage III disease.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with rolled telangiectatic borders and central ulceration on the nasal ala. For this primary nodulo-ulcerative BCC in a high-risk facial location, which treatment modality offers the highest cure rate?
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) offers the highest cure rate (~99% for primary BCC) by enabling complete margin assessment with maximal tissue conservation. It is indicated for BCCs in high-risk locations (nose, eyes, ears, lips - H-zone), morpheaform/infiltrative subtypes, large lesions, recurrent BCCs, and areas where tissue conservation is critical. Standard excision has ~95% cure. Curettage has ~90% but lacks margin control. Topical therapies are only suitable for superficial BCC.

questions.q: A 68-year-old immunocompetent man presents on day 3 of a painful vesicular rash along the right T5 dermatome, not crossing the midline. He has significant allodynia. What is the most appropriate antiviral regimen?
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily for 5 days
Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7-10 days
Valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily for 5 days
No antiviral needed in immunocompetent patients
questions.exp: Herpes zoster: Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day for 7-10 days, OR valacyclovir 1g three times daily for 7 days, OR famciclovir 500mg three times daily for 7 days. Valacyclovir and famciclovir have better oral bioavailability and simpler dosing. Treatment must start within 72 hours of rash onset (earlier is better) to reduce viral shedding, pain duration, and risk of post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN). PHN prevention also benefits from adding gabapentin/pregabalin.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted erosions around the nose and mouth. Several tense bullae are present on the trunk. The bullae contain clear fluid and rupture easily to leave a collarette of scale. What organism is responsible for the bullous variant?
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is caused exclusively by Staphylococcus aureus (phage group II, types 71 and 55), producing exfoliative toxins A and B (ETA and ETB). These serine proteases cleave desmoglein 1 causing intraepidermal (subcorneal) blistering. Non-bullous impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes. Treatment: topical mupirocin or retapamulin for localized disease; oral flucloxacillin/cefalexin for widespread cases.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man with moderate-severe psoriasis (BSA 20%, PASI 18) has failed topical steroids and narrowband-UVB. He is commenced on methotrexate 15mg once weekly. What is the primary monitoring required?
opts: Complete blood count and liver function tests
Renal function tests and urine analysis only
questions.exp: Methotrexate monitoring: CBC (risk of myelosuppression - nadir at 7-10 days; folate supplementation 5mg/week reduces toxicity) and LFTs (hepatotoxicity; check at baseline, then every 4-8 weeks). Traditional liver biopsy at cumulative dose 1.5-2g is now largely replaced by non-invasive markers (FibroScan, FIB-4, PIIINP). Contraindicated in significant hepatic or renal disease, pregnancy, active infection, or bone marrow suppression. Also check renal function at baseline as methotrexate is renally excreted.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic eczematous lesions on the face, scalp, and extensor limbs. Family history of asthma is present. Total serum IgE is 1800 IU/mL with multiple specific IgE sensitizations. Which T-helper cell subset predominantly drives the acute phase and the elevated IgE in atopic dermatitis?
questions.exp: Acute atopic dermatitis is predominantly Th2-mediated: IL-4 and IL-13 drive IgE class switching and impair filaggrin expression (barrier defect); IL-5 causes eosinophilia and mast cell survival. Chronic AD shows a mixed Th2/Th1 profile. This Th2 pathway is the target of dupilumab (anti-IL-4Ra, blocks both IL-4 and IL-13). Th17/Th22 pathways are dominant in psoriasis. Treg cells suppress inflammation and are deficient in atopic diseases.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman on cotrimoxazole for a UTI develops fever, painful erosions on the lips and oral mucosa, conjunctival injection, and genital erosions. Skin shows erythematous macules with dusky centers and epidermal detachment affecting 8% BSA. Skin biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is defined by epidermal detachment <10% BSA with involvement of at least 2 mucosal surfaces, most commonly drug-induced (sulfonamides, aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs, nevirapine). SJS/TEN overlap: 10-30% BSA; TEN: >30% BSA. Full-thickness epidermal necrosis distinguishes SJS/TEN from SSSS (where cleavage is at the granular layer). Immediate drug withdrawal and supportive care in a burns/ICU unit are essential. SCORTEN score guides prognosis.

questions.q: A 26-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic papules and burrows in the interdigital spaces, wrists, belt-line, and genitalia. Pruritus worsens at night. His wife has similar symptoms. Skin scraping confirms Sarcoptes scabiei infestation. What is the first-line topical treatment of choice?
opts: Permethrin 5% cream applied to the whole body for 8-12 hours
Precipitated sulfur 6% ointment nightly for 3 nights
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies - applied from the neck down (including face/scalp in infants), left for 8-12 hours, repeated after 1 week. It is a synthetic pyrethroid with high efficacy and low toxicity, suitable for use in pregnancy and children >2 months. Lindane is avoided due to CNS neurotoxicity. Oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg, two doses 2 weeks apart) is second-line or first-line for crusted (Norwegian) scabies. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with multiple flesh-colored, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules 2-5mm in diameter scattered over the trunk and axillae. Some have a surrounding eczematous halo. What is the causative organism?
opts: Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of Poxviridae
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by MCV (types 1-4), a large double-stranded DNA poxvirus - the largest human-pathogenic virus. Histology shows Henderson-Paterson bodies: large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions compressing the nucleus. The eczematous halo ('molluscum dermatitis') is a local immune response and may signal impending resolution. Transmission: direct skin-to-skin contact, fomites. Self-limiting in immunocompetent children; extensive disease suggests immunodeficiency.

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of vaginal discharge followed by migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the right wrist, and a few painless pustular and papulovesicular lesions on the dorsa of the hands and feet. Blood and cervical cultures are pending. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) complicates 1-3% of N. gonorrhoeae infections, more commonly in women. The arthritis-dermatitis syndrome (Stage 1 DGI) presents with migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and characteristic acral pustular/papulovesicular lesions (2-10 lesions). Cultures of multiple sites (cervix, urethra, rectum, pharynx, blood, skin lesion aspirate) improve diagnostic yield. Treatment: ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM daily until improvement, then step-down to oral cefixime to complete 7-day course.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male develops symmetrically distributed classic target lesions (three concentric zones) on the palms and dorsa of hands 2 weeks after a herpes labialis episode. Only the lips have minimal crust. No systemic symptoms. What is the most common trigger for this recurrent condition?
questions.exp: HSV (types 1 and 2) is the most common trigger for recurrent erythema multiforme minor (EM minor), occurring 7-14 days after a herpes outbreak. HSV DNA is detectable in EM lesions by PCR. EM minor: classic target lesions, <=1 mucosal site, acral distribution. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most common infectious trigger for SJS in children. Drug-triggered cases are classified as SJS/TEN, not EM. Recurrent HSV-triggered EM can be prevented with long-term acyclovir/valacyclovir prophylaxis.

questions.q: A 48-year-old chronic alcoholic man presents with photodistributed blistering, skin fragility, and milia on the dorsa of both hands. Hypertrichosis on the cheeks and hyperpigmentation are also noted. Urine turns pink-red under Wood's lamp. Serum iron studies show elevated ferritin. Urine uroporphyrins are markedly elevated. What enzyme is deficient in the sporadic (acquired) form of this condition?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria, resulting from UROD deficiency (Type I sporadic: acquired inhibition; Type II: autosomal dominant). Risk factors include alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, estrogens (OCP), and iron overload (hemochromatosis). Key features: skin fragility, tense bullae/vesicles on sun-exposed areas, milia, hypertrichosis, hyperpigmentation, sclerodermoid changes. Treatment: phlebotomy (first-line), low-dose hydroxychloroquine, HCV treatment. Ferrochelatase is deficient in erythropoietic protoporphyria (painful photosensitivity, no blistering).

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with vitiligo affecting the face and dorsal hands is found to have elevated TPO antibodies (anti-thyroid peroxidase) and borderline low TSH on routine screening. Which autoimmune condition has the highest association with vitiligo?
questions.exp: Autoimmune thyroid disease is the most common associated autoimmune condition in vitiligo, affecting 15-30% of patients. Both Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease are associated. Vitiligo is also associated with Addison's disease, pernicious anemia (anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies), alopecia areata, and type 1 diabetes - forming part of autoimmune polyglandular syndromes (Schmidt/Carpenter syndromes). Annual thyroid function screening (TFTs and anti-TPO) is recommended for all vitiligo patients.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with a single, well-demarcated, smooth oval patch of non-scarring alopecia on the vertex scalp. Dermoscopy shows yellow dots, black dots, broken hairs, and exclamation-mark hairs at the periphery. Pull test at the margin is positive (easily extracted anagen hairs). What nail change is MOST commonly associated with this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Alopecia areata causes nail changes in up to 30% of patients. The most characteristic change is geometric (grid-like) pitting arranged in regular rows and columns - more regular and superficial than the random irregular pitting of psoriasis. Trachyonychia (rough sandpaper-like nails), leukonychia, and red/spotted lunulae are also seen. Nail involvement may correlate with disease severity and is more common in alopecia totalis/universalis. Exclamation mark hairs (tapered towards the scalp) are pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with fine white adherent scales on the extensor surfaces of the limbs, sparing the antecubital fossae and other flexures. Hyperlinear palmar creases and keratosis pilaris are present. His father has identical findings. Skin biopsy shows absence of the granular layer. What is the mode of inheritance?
questions.exp: Ichthyosis vulgaris is the most common inherited ichthyosis (prevalence 1:250) and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern due to filaggrin (FLG) gene mutations (loss-of-function). FLG is essential for normal skin barrier function and the natural moisturizing factor. Histology shows absent or reduced granular layer. Flexural sparing, hyperlinear palms, and keratosis pilaris are classic. 50% of patients have or develop atopic dermatitis. X-linked ichthyosis (STS gene/steroid sulfatase) is X-linked recessive with normal granular layer.

questions.q: A newborn presents with blisters at birth at sites of minimal trauma. Lesions heal with scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy. By age 3, esophageal strictures develop causing dysphagia. Electron microscopy of perilesional skin shows cleavage in the sub-lamina densa zone. Immunofluorescence antigen mapping is negative for type VII collagen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dystrophic EB (DEB) results from mutations in COL7A1, encoding type VII collagen which forms anchoring fibrils beneath the lamina densa. Sub-lamina densa cleavage on EM is pathognomonic. Scarring, milia, esophageal strictures, pseudosyndactyly (mitten deformity), and increased SCC risk characterize severe recessive DEB. EBS shows intraepidermal cleavage (keratin 5/14 mutations). JEB shows intra-lamina lucida cleavage (laminin-332, integrin mutations). Kindler syndrome has mixed-level cleavage (kindlin-1 mutation).

questions.q: A 58-year-old man has erythematous, poikilodermatous patches on the buttocks, inner thighs, and trunk for 4 years. Skin biopsy shows epidermotropism with haloed atypical lymphocytes, Pautrier microabscesses in the epidermis, and a lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis. Immunophenotyping shows CD3+, CD4+, CD8-, CD7- cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). Pathognomonic features: epidermotropism (single-file arrangement of atypical T-cells in the epidermis) and Pautrier microabscesses (intraepidermal clusters of atypical lymphocytes). Neoplastic cells are CD4+, CD8-, and characteristically lose CD7 (and CD26). Sezary syndrome is the leukemic variant requiring >1000 Sezary cells/uL in blood. Staging: patch-plaque-tumor-erythroderma. TNMB classification guides treatment.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman with severe nodular cystic acne is prescribed isotretinoin. Before initiating therapy, which measure is MANDATORY in this patient?
opts: Ophthalmological examination to rule out night blindness
Negative pregnancy test and commitment to two forms of contraception
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (causes severe craniofacial, cardiac, CNS, and thymic malformations). In women of childbearing potential, a documented negative urine or serum pregnancy test is mandatory before initiation, monthly during treatment, and one month after stopping. Two reliable forms of contraception must be used from 1 month before to 1 month after therapy (iPLEDGE program in the US; similar REMS programs in India). Other routine monitoring includes fasting lipid profile and LFTs at baseline and every 4-6 weeks.

questions.q: A 58-year-old diabetic man presents with all 10 thickened, discolored, crumbly toenails. KOH mount of nail scrapings shows hyphae. Culture confirms Trichophyton rubrum (distal-lateral subungual onychomycosis). What is the most effective systemic antifungal treatment?
opts: Fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for 9-12 months
questions.exp: Terbinafine (an allylamine) 250mg daily for 12 weeks (toenails) or 6 weeks (fingernails) achieves the highest mycological cure rates (~76-80%) for dermatophyte onychomycosis. It is fungicidal against dermatophytes by inhibiting squalene epoxidase. Itraconazole pulse therapy (400mg/day for 1 week/month x 3-4 months) is the alternative. Griseofulvin requires longer treatment with lower cure rates. Ketoconazole is avoided due to severe hepatotoxicity risk. Monitor LFTs in patients with underlying liver disease.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 85 cells/uL presents with painless violaceous plaques on the lower limbs, face, and hard palate. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation, slit-like vascular spaces containing erythrocytes, plasma cells, and extravasated red cells with hemosiderin. What is the causative agent of this condition?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV). AIDS-associated KS (epidemic KS) presents with violaceous lesions on the skin, oral mucosa (palate is classic), GI tract, and lungs. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, plasma cells, and hemosiderin. HHV-8 is also the causative agent of primary effusion lymphoma and multicentric Castleman disease. Treatment: ART restores immune control; pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) for systemic disease; local options include cryotherapy, radiotherapy, intralesional vinblastine.

questions.q: A 72-year-old farmer with decades of outdoor sun exposure presents with a firm, indurated, ulcerated nodule with everted edges on the lower lip. Biopsy confirms well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Which premalignant condition of the lip most directly precedes this SCC?
questions.exp: Actinic cheilitis is the lip equivalent of actinic keratosis - UV-induced dysplasia of the vermilion border of the lower lip (which receives more direct sunlight). Features: blurring/obliteration of the vermilion border, atrophy, erosions, and induration. Malignant transformation to invasive SCC occurs in approximately 10-20%. Treatment: CO2 laser ablation, vermilionectomy (lip shave), or topical 5-FU/imiquimod for in situ disease. Leukoplakia causes intraoral SCC. Actinic keratoses are the SCC precursor on general skin, not the lip specifically.

questions.q: A 46-year-old woman presents with a 10-year history of Raynaud's phenomenon, calcinosis cutis over the fingers, sclerodactyly, facial telangiectasias, and dysphagia. ANA shows a centromere staining pattern. Which antibody is characteristically associated with this clinical phenotype?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are found in 70-90% of patients with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc / CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). ACA is associated with relatively better prognosis but increased risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and primary biliary cholangitis. Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse SSc (dcSSc) and ILD. Anti-RNA Pol III predicts scleroderma renal crisis. Anti-U1RNP is the hallmark of MCTD.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis (on HRZE regimen for 8 weeks) develops bilateral, tender, erythematous nodules on the anterior shins. ESR is 95 mm/hr. Biopsy of a nodule shows septal panniculitis with Miescher's radial granulomas, no vasculitis. What is the most common cause of erythema nodosum in India?
questions.exp: In India, tuberculosis is the most common cause of erythema nodosum (EN), unlike Western countries where streptococcal infection (most common overall) and sarcoidosis (Lofgren syndrome) predominate. EN is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity (septal panniculitis) - a reactive pattern, not a direct infection of the skin. Other Indian causes: leprosy (ENL is a distinct Type III immune complex reaction, not EN), brucellosis, histoplasmosis. Management: treat underlying TB; NSAIDs, potassium iodide, bed rest, compression for symptomatic relief of EN.
